I live in Australia. Unlike most Australians though I have lived in every state and driven between every capital city. I have stayed in many, many rural bum-fuckitty places. I can most definitely confirm that the stereotypes for Aboriginals apply in Australia, but at the same time I can tell you that many Aboriginals break that mold also.

I recall, as a youngster, living in Tindall, NT. The line at Centrelink (Government agency that handles the dole) would start early in the morning. They would live up to collect their cheque then immediately cash it at the bank. After that they headed to the grog shop and bought a case of beer. Once they had their beer they would go to the butcher and buy up chuck meat, which is the meat scraps that one usually buys for their dog. Once they had their supplies they would go to their sleeping ground, usually a tree marked by a pillow/blanket/sleeping bag slung over a low branch. They'd light a fire at their sleeping ground, cook their chuck meat for several hours (because it would be almost inedible without being cooked for ages) in whatever utensil they had and drink warm beer. Once they were done they would pull their blanket down and sleep. Repeat the chuck meat process the next day.

Then there was the time we came across a broken down car and about 8 Aboriginal fellas sitting around it drinking, about 30km's out of town. Dad said he almost pulled over to see if they needed a hand, but the region was notorious for crime so kept going. When we got in to town he went into the police station and told the local cop. His words were (along the lines of): "Yeah that happens every now and then. This region is a dry zone and they're bootleggers. I'll go pick them up tomorrow once they've finished drinking all their grog."

There are more stories of the stereotype of the Australian Aboriginal that I have experienced, like the woman who came to my house seeking refuge and her boyfriend that kicked my door in to bash her. When I called the cops they described the bloke and the woman and when I confirmed it was them they said "He'll stop when she's unconscious. We'll head on over with the ambo's in a bit." - note, this was a town with about an 80% Aboriginal population and the local police were very busy/blase about the whole thing.

I have also seen the good side, like the Aboriginal business man who stood out the front of a club that was popular with the local indigenous population (in Adelaide, Australia) and paid for the cab ride of people who needed to get home but might not be able to afford it. One night a fortnight, without fail. He paid using Cab Charges (a ticket you give to a cabbie linked to a business account that the fare is then charged to). If I remember correctly he was a builder and devoted even more of his time building and repairing the homes of those less fortunate. Incredibly selfless.

Or the TAFE (community college) teacher I had during my apprenticeship. Electrician for a few decades, had built his business from the ground up and handed it on to his sons. He then took up teaching full time as his body was quite worn out from working the really shit jobs in his younger days (Australia doesn't have a history of being racially friendly, despite the image the government portrays internationally, and I can imagine his younger days were fucking terrible for being treated like shit). Despite the fact that he had definitely been wronged at some point, or many points, during his life by the white population of the country he held no resentment towards anyone and obviously worked at it to overcome the hardships to be a successful man. Also possibly the best teacher I had during my apprenticeship, he devoted a lot of individual time to students who needed it. Where other teachers would hand out work then sit down for a couple of hours, he would pace the room and make sure nobody was struggling. Not in an authoritarian manner either, he would chat with us about situations he had been in where the current material applied in the workplace and really put it into perspective. Really, that guy was a legend.

tl;dr: Stereotypes are not something we force upon people, it is something formed based on the typical person that the stereotype describes. If you feel a stereotype has forced you, in any way, to be the person you are then the only truth is that you do not have the strength to break the mold and likely use the stereotype as justification for your behaviours, actions, manners or decisions in life.
